segments.role: Important for denying Netanyahu 61, mainly through Ra'am's threshold, but close to neutral for a change-led government under the formation model, so any investment here is a leadership decision, not a field call.
segments.who: The segment's 38 Negev Bedouin localities hold 144,860 eligible voters, and Arab lists took 94% of their vote in 2022 on 51% turnout. Rahat (38,346 eligible, 61% turnout) is the largest, followed by Tel Sheva, Ar'ara BaNegev, Kuseife, Hura and Laqye at 47-57%. About 40,000 voters from unrecognised villages are assigned by tribe to polling stations 5-65 km from home, where turnout was 38% in 2022 against 56% in recognised Bedouin towns, according to the Abraham Initiatives.
segments.moves: Ra'am won about 74% of the Negev Arab vote in 2022, so Negev turnout bears directly on its threshold risk. The forecast gives Ra'am a 78% chance of passing. Crime and personal safety top Arab voters' concerns, 77% back an Arab party joining the coalition, and young Arab voters want concrete plans on crime, housing, jobs and discrimination. Turnout at the tribal stations has run far below the recognised towns in every recent election.
segments.approach: The change bloc runs no field programme and no branded turnout work here, and the realistic contact plans on this site exclude Arab localities. Under the formation model, each 10,000 extra Ra'am votes moves the chance of a change-led government by about -0.04 points and the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 by about +0.82. Under the deny-61 objective the segment holds about 1,550 net votes at saturation, 14% of that total. Leadership must decide how much weight blocking gets before anything moves. If it decides to support Arab-sector turnout, that support must be independent of the bloc's campaign, transparent and cleared in writing by election counsel. The bloc runs, funds and directs no turnout work here.
segments.message: Any bloc communication that reaches Negev voters should speak to personal safety and fighting crime, concrete plans on housing, jobs and services, and respect for Arab citizens' votes.
segments.messenger: The bloc does not recruit or direct turnout messengers here, and any independent group chooses its own. No bloc-run or bloc-branded turnout activity in these towns. A list's own campaign for its own Arab voters, such as the Democrats' Arabic-language campaign, is that list's decision and goes through its election counsel.
segments.avoid: Avoid any change-bloc rhetoric that treats Arab votes or Arab parties as illegitimate, which can depress Arab turnout. Bloc spokespeople should not make Arab turnout a campaign theme or comment on Arab-sector turnout figures, because Likud plans to use the CEC's station turnout releases to rally its base. The bloc runs no election-day transport or other election-day turnout activity here. Election-day transport, gifts and activity near polling stations are regulated, so check with election counsel.
segments.caveat: Arab-sector turnout is a leadership decision with a real trade-off between objectives, and any support is independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel. In 2019 the CEC chair ruled that a civil-society plan to bus about 15,000 Bedouin voters was politically motivated and let it proceed only if the group registered as a body active in the elections. Funding or in-kind support for another list's or a civil-society group's turnout work therefore needs written approval from election counsel.

segments.role: A small segment with a pocket of direct change-list votes, mostly for the Democrats, whose turnout mainly feeds the Joint List and so helps deny Netanyahu 61 while hurting a change-led government, which makes any investment a leadership decision.
segments.who: Six Christian-majority Galilee villages hold 27,005 eligible voters and turned out 59% in 2022, when Arab lists took 76% and change-bloc predecessors 18.5%. The model projects change lists at 19% in 2026, with the Democrats leading the change vote in every village. Rame (6,574 eligible) projects 28% change and Fassuta, Mi'elya, Eilabun and Jish 21-26%, while Kafar Yasif, the largest (8,257), projects 7%.
segments.moves: Meretz kept a foothold in Christian villages in 2022, with 11.7% against 39.8% for Hadash-Ta'al in Rudnitzky's count. Crime and personal security dominate Arab voters' concerns. The Democrats are the change list best placed to win Arab votes directly. They are touring Arab towns and expanding Arabic social media, and Somaya Bashir of Jatt placed 10th in their primaries (her final list slot is unconfirmed). Ra'am's leader estimates Arab support for Zionist parties at no more than 10-12%.
segments.approach: The change bloc runs no field programme here, and the realistic contact plans exclude Arab localities. At saturation, calls to identified change-list supporters and Rame's two positive stations would be worth about 9 net votes toward a change-led government. General turnout here costs a change-led government. The segment is worth about 127 net votes toward denying Netanyahu 61. The model finds positive door value in only two of Rame's 11 polling stations and none in the other villages, which is too little to justify a programme. The Democrats' own Arabic-language campaign is that list's decision. Any turnout support beyond it is a leadership decision and must be independent, transparent and cleared in writing by election counsel.
segments.message: Personal security and action on crime, equal services, and real Arab representation on a list that can be part of government.
segments.messenger: Local Christian community figures and the Democrats' Arab candidate Somaya Bashir, speaking Arabic.
segments.avoid: Avoid rhetoric that treats Arab votes as illegitimate. One weak 2019 survey experiment found no Jewish backlash to centre-left equality messages aimed at Arab citizens. Even so, bloc spokespeople should not make Arab turnout a campaign theme or comment on Arab-sector turnout figures, because Likud plans to use the CEC's station turnout releases to rally its base. The bloc runs no election-day transport or other election-day turnout activity here. Election-day transport, gifts and activity near polling stations are regulated, so check with election counsel.
segments.caveat: Turnout here adds mostly Joint List votes, which the formation model scores at -0.41 points for a change-led government and +0.75 for denying Netanyahu 61 per 10,000 votes. Any support is a leadership decision and must be independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel.

segments.role: Decisive for denying Netanyahu 61, holding about half of the bloc's blocking potential, but negative for a change-led government under the formation model, so whether to invest is a leadership decision.
segments.who: The segment's 89 Arab localities in the Galilee and the Triangle hold 671,826 eligible voters. Turnout was 54% in 2022 and Arab lists took 93%, and the model projects them at 93% again, with change lists at 6%. The largest low-turnout towns are Nazareth (59,519 eligible, 48% turnout), Umm al-Fahm (38,286, 38%), Baqa al-Gharbiyye (48%) and Shefa-'Amr (51%), while Sakhnin (68%), Tamra (64%) and Tire (62%) already vote at the top of the Arab range.
segments.moves: Arab turnout swings far more than Jewish turnout, between 64.8% in 2020 and 44.6% in 2021. It responds to list configuration, perceived influence, local candidates and backlash against exclusion. In 2022 the southern Triangle, home to top candidates, voted 60.8% against 46.2% in the northern Triangle. Crime is the top issue: about 80% rank it first in Statnet's polling, and 53.5% name it among their top two factors in IDI's August survey. About 77% back an Arab party joining the coalition. The CEC's vote to disqualify both Arab lists, overturned by the Supreme Court on 2 October, may lift turnout, and women and young voters are the largest source of upside.
segments.approach: Change-bloc lists run no turnout programme of their own here, and the realistic contact plans exclude Arab localities. Under the formation model, each 10,000 extra Joint List votes adds about 0.75 points to the chance of denying Netanyahu 61 and costs about 0.41 points of the chance of a change-led government. For Ra'am the figures are +0.82 and -0.04, so if leadership chooses to weight blocking, the model favours Ra'am-majority areas over Joint List areas. Any support must be independent of the bloc's campaign, transparent and cleared in writing by election counsel. The model finds positive door value for change lists in only two of Shefa-'Amr's 54 stations, too few for a programme. Everywhere, the bloc's own job is to keep its messaging from depressing Arab turnout.
segments.message: The bloc's own national messaging should treat Arab citizens and their votes with respect and speak to personal security and crime, which Arab voters rank first, and to services.
segments.messenger: The bloc does not recruit, brief or script messengers for Arab-sector turnout, and any independent group chooses its own. Inside the bloc, the Democrats' Arabic-speaking candidates speak for that list's own campaign, and national spokespeople should address Arab citizens with respect.
segments.avoid: Avoid change-bloc rhetoric that paints reliance on Arab votes as illegitimate, which can deepen alienation. Bloc spokespeople should not make Arab turnout a campaign theme or comment on Arab-sector turnout figures, because Likud plans to use the CEC's station turnout releases to rally its base. This echoes its 2015 message about Arab turnout, and visible threat narratives mobilise the other side. No bloc-run or bloc-branded turnout activity in these towns. A list's own campaign for its own Arab voters, such as the Democrats' Arabic-language campaign, is that list's decision and goes through its election counsel.
segments.caveat: Arab-sector turnout is a leadership decision, and the two objectives point in opposite directions here. Any support is independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel. Funding or in-kind help for another list's or a civil-society group's turnout work raises party-finance questions and, as a 2019 CEC ruling on Bedouin busing showed, can require registration as a body active in the elections. Ghajar, a restricted border village, is not targeted.

segments.role: A candidate-dependent opportunity: about 9% of change-led-government potential and the best yield per contact on paper, but the model's least certain projection, so work waits on a 2026 candidate check and is led by Druze figures on the lists.
segments.who: The segment's 18 Druze and Circassian localities hold 96,043 eligible voters, and turnout was 48.5% in 2022, against 77-79% in 1996-99. Change-bloc predecessors took 68% in 2022, and the model projects change lists at 65% after pooling each village 60% toward the segment average, because 2022 votes followed home-village candidates. Mughar (17,008 eligible) is the largest and the only one where Arab lists lead the projection, while Daliyat al-Karmel, Yirka, Isfiya, Beit Jann and Kisra-Sumei project 61-81% for change lists.
segments.moves: Druze voting is utilitarian and candidate-driven. Almost every party that put a Druze candidate in a winnable slot won that candidate's home village, and kinship and Druze candidates are the strongest predictors of the Druze vote. Home-village peaks run 30-50 points above the Druze average, as with Blue and White's 78.1% in Daliyat al-Karmel in September 2019 and Meretz's 64.8% in Beit Jann in April 2019. In April 2019 a Likud candidate also moved Yirka from the Joint List to Likud. The open grievances are Kaminitz-law fines and demolitions, the planning and housing shortage, and the Nation-State Law. One expert suggests Israel's 2025 moves to protect Druze in Sweida may pull some voters toward Netanyahu, and the research desk found no 2026 Druze poll.
segments.approach: Treat Druze turf as a candidate-dependent opportunity, not a headline. Per contact these villages lead the map (Kisra-Sumei 13.5, Beit Jann 12.7 and Daliyat al-Karmel 10.0 net votes per 1,000 door contacts, against 4.7 in Tel Aviv). The realistic plans rank Daliyat al-Karmel, Beit Jann and Yirka near the top. Before committing volunteer hours, confirm which lists have Druze candidates in winnable slots and run a quick Druze poll. Where the check holds, run in-community supporter contact led by local Druze figures in the eight turnout-engine villages: Daliyat al-Karmel, Beit Jann, Yirka, Kisra-Sumei, Yanuh-Jat, Mughar, Isfiya and Julis. Split turf by lead change list, with Yashar in Daliyat al-Karmel, Yirka, Isfiya and Kisra-Sumei and Yisrael Beytenu in Mughar, Julis and Yanuh-Jat. The Democrats lead Beit Jann's projection only because of a 2022 Meretz home-candidate vote, so assign that turf after the candidate check. In Mughar, work only the stations the model marks positive and skip those where Arab lists lead.
segments.message: Planning and zoning relief, a freeze on Kaminitz-law enforcement while zoning plans are approved, and an equality clause in the Nation-State Law, stated as concrete commitments. Former Blue and White voters need a viable-vote message, since Blue and White polls about 0.6% with about a 1% chance of passing.
segments.messenger: Druze figures with winnable list slots, local notables and family networks. Yashar's Kamil Abu Rokon, a retired Druze general and former Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, is the natural lead if his list slot proves winnable, which has not been verified. Outside volunteers support the work and do not front it.
segments.avoid: Do not message Druze villages as part of the Arab sector, and do not rely on national messaging. Do not headline Druze towns or over-invest before the candidate check, since candidate effects have swung these villages by double digits and a post-Sweida shift toward Netanyahu is an untested risk. Do not plan rides or other election-day transport without election counsel.
segments.caveat: The Druze projection is the least certain in the model. It depends on which lists field Druze candidates in winnable slots in 2026, and pooling only partly removes 2022 home-village votes such as Beit Jann's 62% for Meretz. A stress test that moves 20 points from change to Netanyahu-bloc lists in Druze towns changes 4 of the top 25 localities. The four Golan Druze villages (Majdal Shams, Buq'ata, Mas'ade and Ein Qiniyye) are not targeted, and Hurfeish and Reihaniyye sit in the Lebanon border zone, where capacity is halved.

segments.role: A Netanyahu-bloc stronghold where the bloc runs no door work and the only value is a small amount of list contact with identified change supporters and soft traditional voters.
segments.who: The segment's 28 Haredi localities hold 378,343 eligible voters, and all 28 are rated Netanyahu-bloc strongholds. Turnout was 75% in 2022 and the Netanyahu bloc took 96%, with Modi'in Illit, Betar Illit and El'ad voting at 81-84%. Bnei Brak (115,586 eligible) and Beit Shemesh (78,064, 11% projected change) are the largest. The segment also takes in mixed towns such as Netivot, Safed and Giv'at Ze'ev, where change lists project 13-16%.
segments.moves: Haredi turnout is high and stable, and UTJ's vote has grown at about 95% of the pace of its electorate since 1992. In 2022, 97% of Haredi voters backed the coalition parties. UTJ's chairman was reportedly recorded saying he fears lower turnout after the failed draft-exemption law, though the research desk could not verify the report. A new Haredi Public list splits the vote, and Shas is losing traditional voters to Otzma, Likud and Yashar over the draft crisis.
segments.approach: Run no door canvassing and no general turnout work. The model finds no positive door turf in any station in the segment, because every extra general turnout vote here nets the Netanyahu bloc. It scales persuasion to 15% of normal. The segment's whole value, about 23 net votes at saturation, comes from calls and relational asks to identified change supporters and identified soft traditional voters, mainly in Beit Shemesh, Bnei Brak, Safed and Netivot. Yashar is the lead change list throughout, so its lists should carry this work.
segments.message: Where contact happens, talk to traditional voters about equal burden and the cost of living, with clear respect for religious life.
segments.messenger: Observant and traditional messengers known in the community. Secular change-bloc activists stay out.
segments.avoid: Avoid visible campaigning in Haredi neighbourhoods and draft rhetoric that reads as an attack on Haredim, since both invite counter-mobilisation. Never run activity aimed at lowering anyone's turnout.

segments.role: A Netanyahu-majority city with a large change minority, rated supporter-list ground, where most of the value comes from contacting identified supporters and working a minority of polling stations, not from citywide canvassing.
segments.who: Jerusalem has 432,125 eligible voters and turned out 62% in 2022, when the Netanyahu bloc took 77% and change-bloc predecessors 20%. The model projects 23% change and 73% Netanyahu bloc, with about 6,300 persuadable voters and 2,700 Blue and White or Reservists voters, and Yashar leads the change vote with the Democrats second. The city ranks fifth on the map by change-led-government potential, at about 110 net votes at saturation.
segments.moves: Turnout rose in right-wing strongholds, Jerusalem among them, in 2022. Neighbourhoods differ sharply, and the model finds positive door value in only 129 of the city's 706 stations. Nationally, the draft (26%) and the October 7 inquiry (22%) are decisive for young secular voters. Traditional and moderate religious voters are most likely to respond to equal burden, October 7 accountability and security competence. Among 2022 Likud voters considering a switch, October 7 (37%) and the draft (23%) are the main reasons, and 35% of religious reservists would consider leaving a party that backs draft exemption.
segments.approach: Split the city by polling station and by list. Phone and relational contact is the main channel here, as the tier label says. Door work is a secondary channel limited to the 129 positive stations, where change lists project 35-77%, with Yashar leading most of them and the Democrats the rest. Elsewhere, call and message identified change supporters and hold persuasion conversations with identified soft Netanyahu-bloc voters. The city rises in the realistic plans once supporter lists exist: at 400,000 contacts with 30% of supporters identified it is worth about 83 net votes, third after Tel Aviv and Haifa. Reach Blue and White and Reservists voters through media, digital and list calls timed around the final published polls on Friday 23 October (the publication ban runs from Saturday 24 October), not by knocking on doors.
segments.message: Give traditional and moderate religious voters security competence and equal burden, framed around unity and a broad government. Give secular and young voters the draft and October 7 accountability. Give Blue and White and Reservists voters the threshold arithmetic, with respect for their reservist commitment.
segments.messenger: Right-credentialed figures such as Eisenkot and Bennett, Yashar religious-Zionist figures such as Matan Kahana, and reservists. Left-coded branding belongs only in secular base stations.
segments.avoid: Avoid citywide turnout drives, which net Netanyahu-bloc votes at a projected 73-23 split. Avoid any visible activity in Haredi neighbourhoods that could trigger counter-mobilisation.

segments.role: A reliable change-bloc base of 255 small communities that still turn out below their potential, worth about 165 net votes at saturation. Each is rated low yield on its own, so the work runs through members' own networks rather than door teams.
segments.who: The segment's 255 kibbutzim hold 143,238 eligible voters. Change-bloc predecessors took 83% in 2022 and the model projects change lists at 80%, with the Democrats leading in some, such as Ma'agan Michael, Yagur and Na'an, and Yashar in others, such as Giv'at Brenner and Gesher HaZiv. Turnout was 70% and stayed flat in 2022 while it rose in right-wing strongholds, and kibbutzim turn out about 4 points below comparable localities with the same socio-economic profile.
segments.moves: October 7 hit kibbutz communities directly. Be'eri, Nir Oz and Kfar Aza were still largely displaced in September 2025, and northern border communities were evacuated. On the centre-left, 60% call this the most important election ever, so motivation is high. Contact from friends works even where turnout is already high. One large friend-to-friend texting trial found about 8 points per message received at roughly 76% baseline turnout.
segments.approach: Do not send door teams. No kibbutz is large enough for the realistic plans to deploy one, and most already vote at rates where the model's turnout lift per contact is a fraction of its peak. Mobilise through relational organising instead, with members contacting members through kibbutz movement and regional networks and community WhatsApp groups, and add a vote plan to every contact. Coordinate by lead list, with the Democrats where they lead and Yashar elsewhere. Help displaced members plan travel to their registered polling station (intercity buses and trains are free from 20:00 on 26 October), and confirm any organised transport with election counsel. Reach the segment's 3,900 Blue and White and Reservists voters through media and list calls timed around the final published polls on Friday 23 October (the publication ban runs from Saturday 24 October).
segments.message: Use competitive, high-stakes framing. The 2022 result turned on about 30,000 votes and on lists that missed the threshold. Tie the ask to October 7 accountability and equal burden.
segments.messenger: Fellow members, friends and family, plus trusted regional and movement figures.
segments.avoid: Do not assume the base will turn out by itself, and do not spend on persuasion. Keep change-list rivalry out of kibbutz contact, since moving votes between change lists adds almost nothing unless a list is near the threshold.
segments.caveat: Many kibbutzim, including the Gaza-envelope and Lebanon-border communities, are flagged as displaced and have their capacity halved. Whether the CEC will open special stations for evacuees, as it did with 83 special stations in the February 2025 northern municipal elections, is not yet known.

segments.role: The main turnout engine, holding about 38% of change-led-government potential and the top of every realistic contact plan.
segments.who: The segment's 45 secular, high-SES localities hold 1.36 million eligible voters and turned out 67% in 2022, and the model projects change lists at 65% against 30% for the Netanyahu bloc. Tel Aviv-Yafo (447,576 eligible) alone holds about 581 net votes at saturation, 17% of the national total, followed by Ramat Gan, Herzliya, Kfar Saba and Givatayim. An estimated 36,800 people who voted for change-camp lists in 2021 stayed home in 2022, based on Kolot Nodedim's flow estimates.
segments.moves: Turnout barely moved here in 2022 while it jumped in right-leaning cities. The base is motivated. Change-bloc supporters, now the opposition, say they are more certain to vote than coalition supporters (80% vs 72%), and an N12 analysis puts the bloc's target above 76% turnout among its supporters in the Sharon, Tel Aviv and Haifa. Nationally, the draft (26%) and the October 7 inquiry (22%) are decisive for young secular voters. The segment also holds the largest pool of Blue and White and Reservists voters on the map, about 32,800.
segments.approach: Choose turf station by station. The model marks most stations here positive. The best door efficiency outside the Druze villages is in Tel Aviv (4.7 net votes per 1,000 contacts), Kiryat Tiv'on (3.5), Givatayim (3.1), Caesarea (3.1), Herzliya (2.8), Ramat HaSharon (2.7) and Ramat Gan (2.7). Tel Aviv tops every realistic plan, with about 416 net votes at 150,000 contacts even without supporter lists. Split turf by each station's lead change list. Yashar leads the projection in Tel Aviv and most suburbs, the Democrats lead about a third of Tel Aviv's positive stations, and Together is the usual runner-up elsewhere. Because Yashar's own campaign avoids Tel Aviv, agree in advance which list's volunteers cover its stations there. Concentrate live contact in the last 7-10 days through doors, volunteer phones and relational texting, with a vote plan in every conversation. Send identified supporters one or two SMS reminders 1-3 days before 27 October, in a format confirmed with election counsel and never referring to anyone's voting history. Remind supporters registered at another address, often their parents', that intercity buses and trains are free from 20:00 on 26 October. Reach Blue and White and Reservists voters through media, digital ads and list calls timed around the final published polls on Friday 23 October (the publication ban runs from Saturday 24 October).
segments.message: Use competitive framing. Meretz missed the threshold by about 4,000 votes in 2022, and the Netanyahu bloc came out ahead by about 30,000. For Blue and White and Reservists voters, state the threshold arithmetic with respect. The forecast gives Blue and White about a 1% chance of passing and the Reservists list about 20%, so a vote for either is likely to win no seats.
segments.messenger: Volunteers, and above all friends and family through relational asks. Each list's activists lead in the stations where their list leads. Reservists are the right messengers to voters of the reservist-branded, right-of-centre Reservists list.
segments.avoid: Avoid public boasts about high turnout, which Likud plans to use to rally its base, and 'vote for the biggest party' appeals, which helped sink Meretz in 2022. Do not chase raw low turnout in emigrant-heavy areas, where many registered voters now live abroad. Do not send door teams after Blue and White or Reservists voters, who make up about 2% of a station's voters.
segments.caveat: Station rankings may still favour stations whose low 2022 turnout reflects residents who moved or emigrated, because the model applies one abroad share per locality, so check walk lists against local knowledge. Rescue value is positive under the default objective but turns negative for Reservists voters under the deny-61 objective, because some of them would otherwise vote right.

segments.role: A secondary target where the change-led-government value sits in a few Jewish polling stations and in supporter lists, while the Arab neighbourhoods follow the same leadership rule as the Arab segments.
segments.who: Five mixed Jewish-Arab cities and the village of Neve Shalom hold 219,177 eligible voters and turned out 60% in 2022, when the Netanyahu bloc took 56%, Arab lists 21% and change-bloc predecessors 21%. Lod (58,888 eligible) and Ramla (57,383) project 22% change against 55-60% for the Netanyahu bloc, while Nof HaGalil (35% vs 36%) and Ma'alot-Tarshiha (33% vs 42%) are closer. Yashar leads the citywide change vote in Lod and Ramla, and Yisrael Beytenu in Akko, Nof HaGalil and Ma'alot-Tarshiha.
segments.moves: The Russian-speaking Jewish neighbourhoods of Nof HaGalil and Ma'alot-Tarshiha are Yisrael Beytenu ground. In 2022 Balad was strongest among Arab voters in Lod and Hadash-Ta'al in Akko and Nof HaGalil. Those parties now run together in the Joint List. Crime dominates Arab voters' concerns, while Jewish voters weigh security and the cost of living most.
segments.approach: Work strictly at polling-station level. The model marks 14 of Lod's 103 stations positive, Jewish stations where change lists project about half to 70% of the vote, plus a few in Ma'alot-Tarshiha and Nof HaGalil, while Ramla and Akko have almost none. Run selective door work there. Yisrael Beytenu leads the change vote in all 14 positive Lod stations, all 7 in Nof HaGalil and 7 of 11 in Ma'alot-Tarshiha, so its volunteers should lead this turf, with Yashar taking the few others. Most of the segment's value, about 43 of 54 net votes at saturation, comes from calls to identified change supporters and soft Netanyahu-bloc voters in the rest of these cities. Leave Arab neighbourhoods to Arab lists and civil society. Staff polling committees and observers fully within CEC rules, and remember that since the High Court's 17 September ruling they may not report which identifiable voters have voted.
segments.message: Personal security, crime and the cost of living for everyone. For Russian-speaking voters, add religion-and-state fairness, including civil marriage and equal burden in the draft.
segments.messenger: Russian-speaking Yisrael Beytenu activists, speaking Russian to older voters, and local Jewish community figures for persuasion.
segments.avoid: Avoid citywide turnout drives, which net Netanyahu-bloc votes in Lod and Ramla. Avoid material that sets Jewish and Arab residents against each other, since visible group-threat narratives mobilise the other side.
segments.caveat: Turnout in the Arab neighbourhoods carries the same objective trade-off as the Arab segments. Any support there is a leadership decision and must be independent, transparent and cleared by election counsel.

segments.role: Middle Israel's big swing cities, holding about 15% of change-led-government potential, where turnout and persuasion both pay and station selection decides which to use.
segments.who: The segment's 14 large central and coastal cities hold 982,973 eligible voters and turned out 66% in 2022. The model projects a near tie, 48% change against 47% Netanyahu bloc, with about 17,800 persuadable voters and 17,200 Blue and White or Reservists voters. Haifa (about 174 net votes at saturation), Rishon LeZion (118) and Rehovot (61) are turnout engines, and Petah Tikva (67) is the map's only persuasion battleground.
segments.moves: Rehovot, Petah Tikva, Haifa and Rosh HaAyin are among the cities that track the national result most closely, and pluralities flip here, as in Rishon LeZion and Rosh HaAyin in 2019-20 when Likud mobilised its voters. The swing voters are traditional non-religious and secular Likud voters. The traditional non-religious split 46% Likud to about 31% Yesh Atid and National Unity in 2022. Voters who place themselves in the centre name the economy (40.5%) and the draft (34%) among their top two factors, and undecided voters want cost-of-living relief and less polarisation. Yashar is campaigning along the Route 4 suburbs, Petah Tikva and Rishon LeZion among them.
segments.approach: Split each city by polling station. Run door turnout work in the stations the model marks positive, which cover most of Haifa and Rishon LeZion. Hold persuasion conversations in Petah Tikva, where persuasion is the larger mechanism (about 35 of 67 net votes), and in balanced stations elsewhere. Haifa is second only to Tel Aviv in every realistic plan. Yashar leads almost every positive station and should lead the turf, with Yisrael Beytenu taking the stations it leads in Haifa and Together as the usual runner-up. Message-test soft-right framings online before paid spend, and put paid media into the final 5-7 days. Reach Blue and White and Reservists voters through media and list calls timed around the final published polls on Friday 23 October (the publication ban runs from Saturday 24 October). In politically mixed households, limit turnout contact to confirmed supporters, since partisan turnout appeals spread to other household members.
segments.message: Lead with competence, cost of living and equal burden in the draft, framed around unity and a broad government that includes the centre-right. Concrete information about Eisenkot's and Bennett's records is likely to persuade better than attacks on Netanyahu, whom every voter already knows.
segments.messenger: Right-credentialed messengers such as Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and reservists for soft-right voters, with neighbours and local volunteers rather than candidates at the door.
segments.avoid: Avoid untargeted turnout work in Likud-leaning neighbourhoods, which Likud's own drive targets and where extra turnout nets Netanyahu-bloc votes. Keep left-coded messengers out of persuasion turf.

segments.role: Hundreds of small, mostly change-leaning communities worth about 5% of change-led-government potential, too small and scattered for door teams, so turnout work runs through community networks and phones.
segments.who: The segment's 454 moshavim and rural communities hold 250,807 eligible voters and turned out 73% in 2022. Change lists project 58% against 37% for the Netanyahu bloc, and Yashar leads the change vote in nearly all of them. The segment splits sharply, from Kfar Vitkin (87% projected change) and Giv'at Ela (82%) to Sha'ar Efraim (48%) and Shetulim (29%).
segments.moves: Education, religiosity and income sort these communities more than ethnic origin does. Traditional and right-leaning moshavim are open to the draft wedge, since 60% of reservists who fought in the war would consider not voting for a party that backs exemption, including 48% of right-wing reservists. The segment holds about 6,300 Blue and White and Reservists voters. Soldiers' and reservists' double-envelope votes are counted centrally, so home turnout understates real turnout in some communities.
segments.approach: Use phone and relational contact through community WhatsApp groups and local committees. No moshav is large enough for the realistic plans to send door teams, and driving between small communities is costly. Run turnout contact only in change-leaning communities, and light persuasion with identified voters in balanced traditional moshavim. Yashar leads the change vote in nearly all these communities and should coordinate contact, with the Democrats taking the few where they lead. Reach Blue and White and Reservists voters through media and list calls timed around the final published polls on Friday 23 October (the publication ban runs from Saturday 24 October), not door visits.
segments.message: Equal burden in the draft and reserve duty, security competence and the cost of living. For Blue and White and Reservists voters, the threshold arithmetic, put with respect for their service.
segments.messenger: Neighbours and community members, local council figures and reservists from the community.
segments.avoid: Do not run turnout work in Netanyahu-majority moshavim. Do not read low home turnout in soldier-heavy communities as headroom.
segments.caveat: Many northern and Gaza-border moshavim are flagged as displaced, with capacity halved. Check where residents are living now before planning contact.

segments.role: Netanyahu-majority cities with large change minorities, where value comes mostly from calling identified supporters and persuading identified soft Netanyahu-bloc voters, while untargeted turnout work nets Netanyahu-bloc votes and feeds Likud's own drive.
segments.who: The segment's 33 Likud-leaning cities and development towns hold 1.25 million eligible voters and turned out 63% in 2022. The Netanyahu bloc projects 61% against 36% for change lists. The segment holds the most persuadable voters on the map (about 24,400) and 12.5% of change-led-government potential (about 416 net votes at saturation), more of it from supporter lists than from door work. Netanya, Be'er Sheva, Hadera, Eilat, Tiberias and Dimona are supporter-list ground, Holon is a turnout engine, and Kiryat Motzkin (53% change) and Kiryat Bialik (52%) are among the few places where change lists lead.
segments.moves: Only 58% of 2022 Likud voters said in May they would definitely vote Likud again, and those considering a switch cite October 7 (37%) and the draft (23%). Shas is losing traditional voters to Otzma, Likud and Yashar, and 65% of northern residents say the state is abandoning the north. Likud's own drive targets low-turnout stations where it won about half the vote on about 35% turnout, which it values at 2-3 seats, and a joint Likud-RZP programme ranks stronghold neighbourhoods by turnout and Likud share.
segments.approach: Lead with supporter lists. Identify change supporters first, then call, text and use relational asks to get them out, because door canvassing nets Netanyahu-bloc votes in most stations here. With 30% of supporters identified, Netanya and Be'er Sheva rise near the top of the realistic plans, at about 45 and 33 net votes at 150,000 contacts. Hold persuasion conversations with identified soft Likud and traditional voters, using message-tested scripts. Send door teams only to stations the model marks positive, which cover much of Holon, Kiryat Motzkin and Kiryat Bialik, parts of Netanya and none of Tiberias. Netanya, Be'er Sheva, Hadera, Eilat, Tiberias and Dimona are supporter-list ground, so phone and relational contact is the main channel there and door work is a secondary channel limited to their positive stations. Yashar leads the change vote throughout and should lead the turf, building on its local structures in towns such as Dimona, with Yisrael Beytenu taking the Russian-speaking stations it leads. Reach Blue and White and Reservists voters through media and list calls timed around the final published polls on Friday 23 October (the publication ban runs from Saturday 24 October).
segments.message: Lead with October 7 accountability, security competence and equal burden in the draft, with respect for voters' past Likud loyalty. More voters trust an Eisenkot-led government than Netanyahu to fix the October 7 failures (48% vs 30%). Add local themes of neglect, rebuilding and jobs.
segments.messenger: Right-credentialed messengers, including Eisenkot and Yashar's local organisers, Liberman for Russian-speaking residents, reservists and trusted local figures. Volunteers rather than candidates should knock on doors, and Russian-speaking and Mizrahi communities in the same town need separate messages and messengers.
segments.avoid: Avoid generic turnout drives, which net Netanyahu-bloc votes here and help Likud's Golden Clusters programme. Avoid attacks on Netanyahu or Likud voters, which harden his supporters. Do not read very low turnout in places like central Eilat or Netanya's hotel strip as headroom, since it likely reflects non-resident registration.
segments.caveat: Eilat's raw 2022 turnout (43%) is distorted by people registered there who do not live there, so the model applies a phantom-roll correction and its Eilat figures carry extra uncertainty. Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi and Sderot are flagged as displaced border towns with capacity halved, and almost 40% of Kiryat Shmona's residents had not returned by September 2026.

segments.role: A Netanyahu-bloc stronghold with one narrow persuasion opening among moderate religious-Zionists in mixed suburbs, best served by Yashar's existing operation.
segments.who: The segment's 104 religious-Zionist communities inside the Green Line hold 77,800 eligible voters. Turnout was 77% in 2022 and the Netanyahu bloc took 82%, and most communities are rated Netanyahu-bloc strongholds. Giv'at Shmuel (20,150 eligible, 36% projected change) is the only secondary target, while Yad Binyamin, Nof Ayalon and Bareqet project 8-10% change.
segments.moves: Religious-Zionist voters moved right between 2019 and 2022. An early-September Dialog poll put Yashar and Together at about 7% combined in the sector, with security (35%) and Jewish identity (25%) ahead of the draft (15%). Yashar aims for about two more seats from traditional and moderate religious-Zionist voters through a headquarters under Matan Kahana covering Gush Etzion, Efrat, Giv'at Shmuel and Ariel. Among religious reservists, 35% would consider dropping a party that backs draft exemption.
segments.approach: Run no turnout work, since the segment's turnout value is about 4 net votes in a few Giv'at Shmuel stations. The model scales persuasion to 60% of normal here and the whole segment holds about 15 net votes at saturation, so keep the investment small. Support Yashar's religious-Zionist operation with persuasion conversations with identified moderates in Giv'at Shmuel and in mixed communities such as Hosha'aya. Coordinate so the change lists do not duplicate effort, with Yashar leading in Giv'at Shmuel and Together where it leads, as in Yad Binyamin and Nof Ayalon.
segments.message: Security competence, shared service and equal burden, and respect for Jewish identity, framed around a broad national government.
segments.messenger: Religious-Zionist figures such as Matan Kahana, religious reservists and local community members.
segments.avoid: Avoid secular or left-coded messengers and religion-and-state attacks that read as hostile to religious life. Run no turnout work.

segments.role: Netanyahu-leaning cities with large Russian-speaking communities, where Yisrael Beytenu carries much of the bloc's case and the value is split between selected door turf, supporter lists and persuasion.
segments.who: The segment's 10 Russian-speaking towns hold 580,965 eligible voters and turned out 59% in 2022. The Netanyahu bloc projects 57% against 40% for change lists, and the segment holds about 193 net votes at saturation, roughly 54% from turnout, 38% from persuasion and 8% from rescue. Ashdod (181,784 eligible, 35% change) is rated a turnout engine on its selected stations, Bat Yam (51% turnout, 43% change) is supporter-list ground, and Karmiel (53%) and Nesher (54%) lean to the change lists.
segments.moves: Russian speakers are about 15% of the population and 50-60% secular. Adult 1990s immigrants lean right, while the Israeli-born generation votes like other Israelis, and Likud voters are split on religion-and-state questions such as civil marriage. Yisrael Beytenu has mapped the neighbourhoods and polling stations where Likud did best and is concentrating on Russian-speaking ex-Likud voters. The research desk found no 2026 poll of Russian speakers, so the model leans on past results.
segments.approach: Work at polling-station level. Send door teams to the stations the model marks positive, about 40% of Ashdod's and half of Bat Yam's, and most of Karmiel's, Nesher's, Kiryat Yam's and Arad's. Call identified supporters elsewhere, and run persuasion with identified ex-Likud voters in Likud-leaning stations of Ashdod and Ashkelon. Split turf by lead list. Yisrael Beytenu leads nearly half the positive stations in Ashdod and a third in Bat Yam, and leads Kiryat Yam, Migdal HaEmek and Arad outright, while Yashar leads the rest. Contact older and 1990s-immigrant voters in Russian through Russian-speaking volunteers, and keep separate messages and messengers for the Mizrahi and Russian-speaking communities of the same town.
segments.message: Religion-and-state fairness, including civil marriage and equal burden in the draft, plus security competence and the cost of living.
segments.messenger: Liberman and Yisrael Beytenu's Russian-speaking activists, Russian-language media and community figures.
segments.avoid: Avoid Hebrew-only material for older voters, and untargeted turnout work in Ashdod and Ashkelon, where the Netanyahu bloc projects 61-63%. Discount raw low turnout, which may partly reflect emigrants and elderly residents.
segments.caveat: The model's data predate immigrants who arrived from Russia and Ukraine after 2022, so newer Russian-speaking voters are not reflected in these projections.

segments.role: A Netanyahu-bloc stronghold with no field work beyond Yashar's existing religious-Zionist outreach.
segments.who: The segment's 82 national-religious West Bank settlements hold 101,984 eligible voters. Turnout was 75% in 2022 and the Netanyahu bloc took 91%, and the model projects 85% for the Netanyahu bloc and 13.5% for change lists. Efrat (7,945 eligible, 18% projected change) is the largest, and Bet El (6%) and Kiryat Arba (10%) are the least open of the larger settlements.
segments.moves: RZP took about 60% of the vote east of the separation barrier in 2022, and security and Jewish identity lead the sector's concerns. Yashar's Kahana-led headquarters covers Efrat and Gush Etzion. Soldiers' double-envelope votes are counted away from home, and adding them back lifts Judea and Samaria turnout by about 10 points, so recorded turnout understates real turnout.
segments.approach: Run no turnout work and no change-bloc field operation. The model finds almost no positive door turf, and the segment's whole value is about 12 net votes at saturation, from list contact. Leave the narrow opening in Efrat and Gush Etzion to Yashar's religious-Zionist team, using phone and relational contact with identified moderates, and coordinate with Together, which leads the change vote in Efrat, Bet El and Elkana.
segments.message: Security competence, equal burden and a broad national government that respects religious life.
segments.messenger: Religious-Zionist figures and local residents connected to Yashar's operation.
segments.avoid: Avoid visible secular campaigning, which can provoke counter-mobilisation. Never treat low recorded turnout as headroom.

segments.role: A low-yield segment of secular and mixed West Bank localities, where what little value there is comes from persuasion in Ariel and Ma'ale Adumim and from a few change-leaning communities near the Green Line.
segments.who: The segment's 32 secular and mixed West Bank localities hold 78,737 eligible voters and turned out 70% in 2022. The Netanyahu bloc projects 58.5% against 38% for change lists. Ma'ale Adumim (28,142 eligible, 24% change) and Ariel (39%) are the largest, while Kfar HaOranim (74%), Har Adar (66%), Oranit (53%) and Alfei Menashe (52%) lean to the change lists.
segments.moves: Secular settlements west of the barrier are Likud and Yisrael Beytenu territory. Yashar's religious-Zionist headquarters covers Ariel. The draft is a strong wedge with right-leaning reservist communities, since 48% of right-wing reservists would consider not voting for a party that backs exemption.
segments.approach: Keep the effort small. The whole segment holds about 22 net votes at saturation, and persuasion supplies most of it (about 16). Run persuasion calls with identified voters in Ariel (Yisrael Beytenu leads) and Ma'ale Adumim (Yashar). Oranit and Alfei Menashe, where Yashar leads, are large enough for a short door canvass of their positive stations, which the model values mainly for persuasion, with rescue left to media and list calls. Reach Har Adar and Kfar HaOranim through relational contact.
segments.message: Security competence, equal burden in the draft and reserve duty, and the cost of living.
segments.messenger: Yisrael Beytenu and Yashar local activists, reservists and residents.
segments.avoid: Avoid citywide turnout work in Ariel and Ma'ale Adumim, where the Netanyahu bloc projects 58-74%. Do not read low home turnout in soldier-heavy communities as headroom.
